stories.text: The Wilford Village and Wilford Lane stops, on line 2 from the city centre to Clifton, opened in August 2015.

Coal was found on the Clifton estate, and work on Clifton Colliery began in 1868. Sir Robert Juckes Clifton, the last of the Clifton baronets, died of typhoid in 1869; the colliery and this toll bridge, both his projects, opened in 1870.

For some 400 years a ferry crossed the Trent here, until a temporary wooden footbridge replaced it in 1864. On 16 June 1870 the toll bridge opened, and pedestrians paid a halfpenny to cross; it is still known locally as the Halfpenny Bridge. It was closed to traffic in 1974, and in 1980 its centre span was replaced by a narrower footbridge. In 2014–15 it was widened again to carry the trams of Nottingham Express Transit, and it is now a tram, pedestrian and cycle bridge.

69731.sum: Wilford Toll Bridge, locally referred to as the 'Halfpenny Bridge', is a tram, pedestrian and cycle bridge in Nottingham, England. It crosses the River Trent between the Meadows and Wilford. It originally opened as a toll bridge for general traffic in 1870, but was closed when declared unsafe in 1974.

stories.text: Fellows Morton & Clayton, who ran the largest fleet of barges and narrowboats in the country, built this canalside depot in 1895. Boats loaded and unloaded at the wharf beside it; the building is now a pub, and listed Grade II.

stories.text: Authorised in 1792 and engineered by William Jessop, the canal opened in 1796 from the Trent to Langley Mill, bringing coal to the town. Railways took its trade; most of the main line was abandoned in 1937.

72555.sum: Canal Museum, on Canal Street. Today it houses Canalhouse. The building was built in 1895, according to OpenStreetMap. It is Grade II listed.

stories.text: Nottingham's first station, opened in 1839 by the Midland Counties Railway, stood across Carrington Street; a through station replaced it on this site in 1848. The present building, of red brick and terracotta, was designed by the local architect Albert Edward Lambert and opened on 16 January 1904. Its carriage entrances have Art Nouveau gates of wrought iron. A pair taken down in 1951, made in Leicester in 1904, is now in the Science Museum Group's collection.[^gates]

72578.sum: Nottingham station, briefly known as Nottingham City and for rather longer as Nottingham Midland, is a railway station and tram stop in the city of Nottingham, England. It is the principal railway station of Nottingham. It is also a nodal point on the city's tram system, with a tram stop that was originally called Station Street but is now known as Nottingham Station.

stories.text: The tunnel was meant to let carriages from the Park reach Derby Road through the sandstone. It was begun in about 1844 and finished by T. C. Hine in 1855–56, but at 1 in 12 it was too steep for horses and carriages, so it became a footway.[^walk] It runs from Tunnel Road to Derby Road, with steps halfway up to Upper College Street.

73655.sum: The Park Tunnel is a residential building on Park Terrace. The building was built in 1881, according to OpenStreetMap, though other sources give a different date. It is Grade II listed as Numbers 18, 19 and 20 and Attached Railings and Retaining Wall to Park Tunnel and was designed by Thomas Chambers Hine.

stories.text: Nottingham Victoria, the Great Central and Great Northern railways' station, opened on 24 May 1900 and closed on 4 September 1967. It was demolished except for its clock tower, which still stands at the entrance of the Victoria Centre built on the site.

75086.sum: Nottingham Victoria station: a takeaway. The building was built in 1899, according to OpenStreetMap. It is Grade II listed as Victoria Centre Clock Tower and was designed by Albert Edward Lambert.

stories.text: A shopping centre opened in 1972 on the site of Nottingham Victoria railway station, whose clock tower still stands beside it.

75088.sum: Victoria Centre: a shopping centre on Victoria Centre. The building was built in 1972, according to Wikipedia.

stories.text: E. P. Davis built the Bennerley furnaces, near Ilkeston, in about 1870; by 1880 they belonged to the Awsworth Coal and Iron Company, which was putting up a new furnace.[^grace] A branch of the viaduct's railway served the works. They made their last pig iron in March 1931, and in 1934 Thos. W. Ward of Sheffield bought the three furnaces to take them down.[^grace] The pin is approximate.

In 1876–77 a viaduct was built here of wrought iron, light enough for ground undermined by coal workings. It closed in 1968 but was too costly to take down, and in 2022 it reopened to walkers and cyclists. The only other viaduct like it is Meldon Viaduct in Devon.

147205.sum: Bennerley Viaduct is a former railway bridge, now a foot and cycle bridge, between Ilkeston, Derbyshire, and Awsworth, Nottinghamshire, in central England. It was completed in 1877 and carried the Great Northern Railway's Derbyshire Extension over the River Erewash, which forms the county boundary, and its wide, flat valley. The engineer was Samuel Abbott, who worked under Richard Johnson, the GNR's chief engineer.

stories.text: In 1832 coal owners meeting at the Sun Inn, Eastwood, proposed extending the Mansfield and Pinxton Railway to Leicester. It became the Midland Counties Railway, whose line from Nottingham, at Carrington Street, to Derby opened in 1839.

stories.text: Nottingham Corporation Tramways built the depot in 1900 when it carried the Carrington tram line on up Mansfield Road to Winchester Street. Trams ran until 6 September 1936, when buses replaced them. Part of the building is now the Samuel Hall pub, named after the man who laid out Sherwood.

Gedling's railway station closed on 4 April 1960, though coal trains ran to the colliery for decades more. Its building is now a youth centre, and there are plans to reopen the line or make it a cycleway.

260511.sum: Gedling and Carlton railway station was a former railway station built to serve the villages of Gedling and Carlton in Nottinghamshire.

stories.text: Trolleybuses, buses drawing power from overhead wires, first ran on 10 April 1927 and took over the tram routes one by one; the last tram ran in September 1936.[^s1] A depot opened on Parliament Street in June 1929 and is still in use.[^s2] By the end of 1937 the city had 125 trolleybuses, the largest fleet in the country, and at most 157.[^s2] The last ran on 30 June 1966.[^s1]

stories.text: Licensed in 1929 and opened in 1930 by Sir Sefton Brancker, it was one of Britain's first municipal aerodromes. In the Second World War it repaired Lancaster bombers; its 18 concrete pillboxes are all listed. The airfield closed on 6 June 2025, sold to the Vistry Group to build 4,000 houses.[^village]
